N1.name: Basic monitoring and a service inventory
N1.manager: Within a month, build an inventory of core services (name, owner, dependencies) and make sure every service has at least liveness and error-rate monitoring.

engineer.week: List the services you own and their current monitoring.
engineer.pitch: "I put together a service list. Three services have no monitoring at all; I'd like to schedule time to fix that."

N2.name: Define SLIs for core services
N2.manager: Pick the one or two services that matter most to users and, together with product, define two SLIs: success rate and latency. Measure first; don't set targets yet.

engineer.week: Compute one service's success rate and p95 latency from load balancer or access logs.
engineer.pitch: "I can compute the success rate from the logs we already have, no new tools. Shall we look at a month of numbers first?"

N3.name: Set SLOs and dashboards
N3.manager: Use a month of measurements as the baseline for a first SLO, put it on a shared dashboard, and schedule a quarterly review.

engineer.week: Build a one-page dashboard showing only SLI vs. SLO.
engineer.pitch: "Our success rate over the last month was 99.7%, but the doc says 99.9%. Can we reconcile that?"

N4.name: Calculate and regularly review the error budget
N4.manager: Spend a fixed five minutes in the monthly review on the remaining error budget, and record whether it influenced any decision.

engineer.week: Calculate this month's remaining error budget and post it in the team's weekly meeting.
engineer.pitch: "We have 20% of the budget left this month. Should we hold off on next week's big release?"

N5.name: Error budget policy
N5.manager: Co-sign a one-page policy with product and engineering leads: when the budget runs out, freeze feature releases, prioritize reliability work, and agree on an exception process.

engineer.week: Draft a one-page policy and bring it for discussion.
engineer.pitch: "We have no agreement on what happens when the budget runs out, so the next conflict will still go to whoever is loudest. I wrote a one-page draft."

N6.name: Incident severity levels and roles
N6.manager: Define three severity levels and two fixed roles, incident commander and communications lead, and write them up as a one-page incident process.

engineer.week: Volunteer as scribe in the next incident and record the timeline.
engineer.pitch: "We split up roles ad hoc in every incident. Can we at least define who the incident commander is?"

N7.name: Clear service owners and on-call
N7.manager: Assign every core service one owner and an on-call rotation shared by the development team.

engineer.week: Check whether your services' owner fields are out of date and list the gaps.
engineer.pitch: "Nobody is sure who to wake up if these three services break at night. I made a list."

N8.name: Blameless postmortems with action item tracking
N8.manager: Adopt a blameless format and put action items in the real backlog (with owners and deadlines); review the closure rate monthly.

engineer.week: Turn the action items from the last incident into tickets.
engineer.pitch: "Nobody has picked up the five action items from the last incident, so I created tickets for them."

N9.name: Alert inventory and cleanup
N9.manager: Next quarter, assign an owner to review every page from the past 30 days and remove or downgrade alerts that need no action. Target: more than 50% actionable.

engineer.week: Export your pages from last month and mark the ones that didn't need any action.
engineer.pitch: "70% of last month's pages needed no action. I'd like two days to clean up our alerts."

N10.name: SLO burn rate alerts
N10.manager: Switch core services to multi-window burn rate alerts instead of plain threshold alerts.

engineer.week: Build a burn rate alert for one service and run it alongside the old alerts for a month.
engineer.pitch: "I'd like to trial a burn rate alert on one service for a month, in parallel, without touching the existing alerts."

N11.name: Progressive delivery and fast rollback
N11.manager: Start with one service: introduce canary or blue-green releases and rehearse a rollback, aiming to recover within 15 minutes.

engineer.pitch: "A rollback takes 40 minutes today. I can script the steps first and aim to get it down to 15."

N12.name: Measure toil and reserve time to remove it
N12.manager: Within a month, measure the share of toil from tickets or on-call records, and reserve a fixed share of every sprint for eliminating it.

engineer.week: Log all repetitive manual work for one week.
engineer.pitch: "30% of my time this week went to repetitive work. Here are the top three; I'd like to schedule automating one."

N13.name: Spread incident learning
N13.manager: Hold a monthly cross-team incident share and track recurring causes.

engineer.week: Post a key takeaway from the last postmortem to a shared channel.
engineer.pitch: "Could we set aside 30 minutes a month to take turns sharing one incident?"

N14.name: Correlated observability (metrics, logs, traces)
N14.manager: Give core services standard dashboards and a unified request ID so metrics, logs and traces can be correlated.

engineer.week: Add a shared trace ID to one service's logs and traces.
engineer.pitch: "I have to open four tools when something breaks. With a trace ID I can connect them in one step."

N15.name: Change traceability
N15.manager: Have every deployment write a change record automatically, linkable to incidents.

engineer.week: Overlay deployment markers on the dashboards.
engineer.pitch: "When something breaks we don't know what changed recently. I can start by overlaying deploy events on the graphs."

N16.name: Shared automation and IaC
N16.manager: Create a shared, version-controlled automation library and require infrastructure changes to go through IaC.

engineer.week: Move scattered scripts into a shared repo and add a README.
engineer.pitch: "We have seven scripts living on personal laptops. I'd like to collect them in one repo."

N17.name: Manage on-call health
N17.manager: Track night pages and rotation fairness, and set rules that trigger changes when limits are exceeded.

engineer.week: Record your night pages for a month.
engineer.pitch: "I was woken up 9 times at night in the past month. Can we look at how to bring that down together?"
